name: Waterless skincare

lead: Waterless, or anhydrous, skincare means products formulated without water: oils, balms, powders and solid bars. The term has been used in beauty media since at least 2018.
People use it for a hydrated, nourished-looking complexion; supporters say that without water the active ingredients make up more of the product, and that oils help hold moisture on skin.

paras: Common formats are cleansing and facial oils, balms, powder cleansers and powders such as vitamin C that are mixed into a serum, and solid shampoo or lotion bars. People swap them in for water-based cleansers and moisturisers.
Waterless products can cost more, since water is a cheap filler. Heavy oils and balms may not suit every skin type, and the usual cosmetic cautions about irritation apply.

web.title: Waterless products: the next wave in beauty (BeautyMatter)

chain: Use oil, balm, powder or bar products instead of water-based ones
Higher concentration of actives; oils seal in moisture
angle.text: Waterless products are used as cleansers and moisturisers, with the aim of delivering concentrated actives and keeping skin hydrated.

lead: Waterless beauty refers to anhydrous products that contain no water. A 2018 industry article described formats including oils, balms, powders and bars.[1]

Supporters list several claimed benefits: without water, formulas are more concentrated so less is needed; anhydrous products can be naturally self-preserving; and oils may trap water on the skin for longer-lasting hydration. The same article notes that waterless products can cost more because water is an inexpensive base.[1]
Sustainability is a major theme in the marketing, tied to water footprint and reduced packaging and transport.[1]

paras: Oils include cleansing oils and moisturisers made with almond, jojoba or rosehip; balms blend oils and waxes to hydrate dry skin and remove makeup; powders are mostly cleansers for gentle exfoliation plus actives such as vitamin C; bars include soap, shampoo, conditioner and lotion in minimal packaging.[1]

Proponents say water is a cheap filler that requires preservatives, that anhydrous formulas can use concentrated antioxidants and that oils keep water on the skin longer.[1] The article also says higher concentration reduces packaging and transport costs but can raise product price.[1]

timeline.event: Industry press describes waterless products as the next wave in beauty.[1]
